chapter_theme: Udayanan reaches Magadha still grieving, is deceived by a promise of his lost queen, is joined to Padmavati, and then Urumannuvan, Yugi's model in mind, turns the threat of seven kings into a stratagem of disguise and rumour.

151.reading: The king leaves the Jayanti border, travels on into the Magadha country, and arrives at dawn; grieving in heart for his queen even as his ministers console him, he enters a harsh forest.
151.nuance: The subject is never named in the verse; the king is known from the story so far, and the sense of line 3 (his love for the queen weighing on him despite comfort) is not fully fixed.
151.event: Udayanan crosses into the Magadha country and enters the forest, still grieving for the queen.

152.reading: Hoping the dead queen may yet be brought back, the king heads that way; seeing a stag with its doe and a peacock dancing, he weeps and speaks of his lost wife.
152.nuance: The verse calls the queen dead (செத்த) yet lets him hope to bring her back; the hope comes from the earlier plan and is not explained here.
152.event: Udayanan, going toward Magadha, weeps at the sight of paired animals and a dancing peacock.

153.reading: The king, who cannot walk on, points to flowers on branches and creepers as showing his queen's adornment; he climbs a hill, passes the forest and reaches rich Magadha.
153.nuance: Grief makes every sight a likeness of the lost wife; the same habit of seeing her in other things returns in verse 157.
153.event: Udayanan sees flowers as the queen's ornament, climbs a hill, crosses the forest and reaches Magadha.

154.reading: Maran, commander of the army of Tarusakan, lord of the Magadhas, lives in splendour in the town of Rajagiri, just outside the capital.
154.nuance: The verse only places Maran and Tarusakan; it gives no action of the king himself.
154.event: Maran, the Magadha king's army commander, is settled at Rajagiri outside the city.

155.reading: At the Kamakottam gate, among ascetics of the Soma sort, Vayantakan finds the learned brahmin Kakatundan and tells him a deceitful tale.
155.nuance: The deceit is named but its content is not given; the verse is the start of a plan, not a statement of belief.
155.event: Vayantakan meets Kakatundan in the ascetics' hall and feeds him a false story.

156.reading: The brahmin meets the king and says that if he stays in this town for two months he will restore the lost queen and the earth with her; meanwhile the Magadha king's sister appears one day.
156.nuance: The promise is part of the deceit begun in verse 155 and answers the king's hope in verse 152; the verse breaks off before the sister's coming is told.
156.event: Kakatundan promises the king the lost queen and the earth if he waits two months.

157.reading: Padmavati, in full bloom, drives up in a chariot to see the god of love himself; the king, seeing her, is glad and says that Vasavadatta has come, and the lady stands troubled at the sight of him.
157.nuance: The king's eyes mistake Padmavati for the dead wife because his mind is full of her; compare the flowers he took for her ornament in verse 153.
157.event: Padmavati comes in a chariot, and Udayanan takes her for Vasavadatta.

158.reading: Padmavati's friend Yappiya Iniyal goes to the king, praises her charms and brings them together; protected by his guards, the king unites with her.
158.event: Yappiya Iniyal brings Padmavati to the king and they unite.

159.reading: After joining her at Kamakottam as nature has it, the Vatsa king tells his ministers sweetly that he will not leave the nectar-voiced girl for desire; they bow and say 'may you gain enjoyment, appear'.
159.nuance: The ministers' reply (line 4) is brief and its last word is not clear; they appear to approve the king's pleasure.
159.event: Udayanan tells his ministers he will not leave Padmavati, and they bless the match.

160.reading: Riding a splendid palanquin with the girl into a mansion, the king shows her the lute, which he has kept hidden; the angry Urumannuvan is moved to speak of this.
160.nuance: The cause of Urumannuvan's anger is not given in the verse; the verse prepares his speech in verse 161.
160.event: Udayanan takes Padmavati to a mansion and shows her the lute; Urumannuvan, angered, speaks.

161.reading: Yugi, whose mind is kind and who knows events, freed Kunjai from prison and left with the queen; so Urumannuvan proposes that they too go, after the king has been married afresh to this girl.
161.nuance: The speaker is Urumannuvan only because verse 160 ends by saying he will speak; verse 161 does not name him. The model he cites is Yugi's earlier escape from Ujjain, told in the preceding kandam.
161.event: Urumannuvan proposes that the king be married to Padmavati before they all leave.

162.reading: Urumannuvan sends three hundred kinsmen, who by their art slip unseen into the king's palace while the king, unable to find the great treasure his father laid up, searches for those who moved it.
162.nuance: Line 4 can be read as the king looking for the thieves of the treasure; the verse does not say that Urumannuvan's men took it.
162.event: Urumannuvan's three hundred men hide in the Magadha palace while the king hunts for his father's lost treasure.

163.reading: A speaker says he will tell what he knows, meets the king and shows him a great treasure; thereafter the Magadha king, with goodwill, lives happily beside Urumannuvan, who is never parted from him, by means of his art.
163.nuance: The verse does not name who says 'I will tell what I know'; the story points to Urumannuvan, but the speaker is a guess, and line 4 (பானலங் கிளவி) is also hard to place.
163.event: Urumannuvan shows Tarusakan a great treasure and the two live as close allies.

164.reading: Seven kings, among them the lord of Ayodhya's army chief Shali, Palamuru Sakti, Mudiviri Sikaiyan and Mukatteli Seviyan, come together to Magadha.
164.nuance: The names are listed by title; some of them are hard to separate (the verse mixes names and nicknames).
164.event: Seven allied kings of the forest and Ayodhya arrive in Magadha with their forces.

165.reading: The seven, angry, say they will not pay tribute to Tarusakan and come to destroy his pleasant land; he is shaken at the news, and Urumannuvan says that he will break them by a stratagem.
165.nuance: The verse prefers plan (உபாயம்) to open battle for the defence; line 4's first words are hard to parse.
165.event: The seven kings refuse tribute and march to ravage Magadha; Urumannuvan promises to defeat them by stratagem.

166.reading: In disguise, Urumannuvan and the king, joined by his wit to the Magadha king, go as merchants who sort jewels, swap a few, and set up a shop in the enemy camp selling many gems.
166.nuance: Line 1's 'false form' and 'merchant form' suggest a change of guise for both; the jewels are a pretext for getting inside the camp.
166.event: Urumannuvan and Udayanan, disguised as jewel merchants, set up a stall in the enemy camp.

167.reading: In an unclear verse, words the king and the Magadhas would not wish to hear spread among the troops as they come into the four-fold camp by night, hidden talk of many kinds.
167.nuance: The verse is in a different, shorter metre and its words are broken; the reading is a guess.
167.event: Hidden rumours spread through the camp at night.

168.reading: Those who heard the talk lose heart, the troops give way and run, and the enemy leaders gather in confusion, until the doubt in their minds is gone.
168.nuance: Line 4 (ஐயம் மனத்திடை நீங்கினார்) is hard: it can be read as the leaders' doubt ending, or as their giving up their purpose.
168.event: The rumours break the enemy's nerve and its army runs.

links.note: The brahmin's promise of the lost queen meets the king's hope in verse 152.
links.teaches: The promise is aimed at a hope the king already holds, so the deceit works because it answers his grief.

links.note: In both verses the king sees the dead queen in something else, first flowers and then Padmavati.
links.teaches: A habit of seeing her likeness in things turns from a poet's sorrow into a real mistake that begins the new marriage.

links.note: The treasure the king searched for in verse 162 is shown to him in verse 163.
links.teaches: The king's loss is turned into Urumannuvan's service, so the search sets up the trust that follows.

links.note: The seven kings named in verse 164 now make their demand and march on the land.
links.teaches: The list of names becomes a real threat only when they refuse tribute, which is what makes the stratagem necessary.

links.note: The disguise as merchants carries out the stratagem Urumannuvan promises in verse 165.
links.teaches: The stratagem is a trade, not a battle, which tells the reader how Urumannuvan means to win.

links.note: Disguised ministers sell jewels in an enemy camp, as the Kural describes a spy who takes an unsuspected form.
links.teaches: The epic's spies are the king and his own minister, and gems are the means, which the Kural's spy has no word for.

gains.a: The verse gains a rule, a spy's form must raise no suspicion, which shows why the jewel trade is chosen as the disguise.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which king and minister both act as the spy, which its plain listing of the spy's duties does not offer.

cast.role: the king of Vatsa, in exile in Magadha
Udayanan's minister who planned the escape from Ujjain
the learned brahmin of the Soma ascetics' hall who is deceived and then promises the king his queen
the three hundred kinsmen Urumannuvan sends
the seven allied kings who march on Magadha

source_issues: Verses 167 and 168 are in a different, shorter metre and lines are broken; the readings are tentative.
Verse 163 lines 3 to 4 are hard to parse; the speaker of line 1 is not named.
Verse 161: the speaker is inferred from the last line of verse 160.
